paper_title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81\% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Mathematical modeling contests such as CUMCM in China and MCM/ICM internationally ask teams *Equal Contribution Corresponding Author 1 to convert deliberately under-specified real-world problem into defensible quantitative answer within days. The deliverable is not single number but chain: assumptions model solution sensitivity recommendation. Two properties make it an attractive target for agent evaluation: it is quantitative, because the final question ends in numbers that can be checked, and it is multimodal, because statements reference figures and attachments are spreadsheets and CSVs. It also differs from solving well-posed problem in where the hard work beginsthe model itself must be built, and the same situation admits time-series, optimization, dynamical, graph, or multi-criteria formulations, any of which can be defensible if its assumptions are explicit and its computation credible (Giordano et al., 2014; Meerschaert, 2013). This is what makes modeling demanding test of long-horizon agents: hold the statement and attachments in context, choose formulation, write and run code, handle files and units, and report self-consistent answer. Existing benchmarks cover adjacent but distinct ground, and none closes the loop we care about. Code, terminal, and assistant benchmarks score repository edits, command-line competence, and tool use (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; Mialon et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025); closed-form mathematics benchmarks score deduction rather than modeling (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Cobbe et al., 2021; Glazer et al., 2024); operations-research datasets parse word problems into solver-ready formulations (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). The closest prior work on modeling itself falls into two camps, neither simultaneously agentic, verifiable, terminal, and multimodal. One stays solver-facing and narrow, scoring single formal artifact (Huang et al., 2025b). The other grades the final report with an LLM judge (Qian et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), rewarding fluent prose without establishing that the reported numbers are correct or even admissible. Table 1 makes the gap concrete; TB-MathModel is the first to combine all of these properties. Closing the gap raises three problems that shape the design. Different teams make different assumptions, so there is no single ground truth: rather than promote one paper to truth, TB-MathModel asks every human expert, scoring each task against panel of outstanding solutions so that model must be close to many accepted answers, not match one. Anchoring creates asymmetric failurea model that does better than the paper can score worse than one that copies itso TB-MathModel makes each metrics direction explicit and scores one-sidedly. And wrong-but-plausible answer is easy to produce (numbers that look reasonable yet violate the problems physics), which anchor comparison cannot catch, so TB-MathModel adds an independent feasibility layer. We present TB-MathModel (Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), to our knowledge the first benchmark to turn complete contest-style mathematical modeling problems into an agentic, verifiable, terminal evaluation. It contributes: 1. The first benchmark of its kind, and the 18task dataset behind it. No prior benchmark turns complete contest-style modeling problems into containerized terminal task with an executable verifier. TB-MathModel covers CUMCM and MCM 20232025 (problems A/B/C each year), with verbatim statements, official attachments, 21 figures cropped from the PDFs, and one JSON artifact per task. 2. Direction-aware, one-sided scoring with auditable edge-case rules. Per-metric semantic directions (higher/lower_is_better, target_value, exact_value); two reported metrics (O-EVAL, ROBUST BO-EVAL); explicit rules for degenerate bands and unpinned reference units; and contract tests that lock the two defining properties down. 3. two-layer feasibility verification design. programmatic gate covering 18/18 tasks through six decidable invariant forms, and Lean 4 certificate layer of 624 kernel-checked obligations; the two layers decide every feasibility question structured artifact can settle, and state exactly where an independent replay takes over. 4. An empirical study of seven multimodal model/harness entries, each averaged over three seeds, with per-task behaviour, cost robustness analysis, and three case studies; we also document the scoring pitfalls we found and fixed and quantify which move the leaderboard. Against the human panel, the two newest flagships lead (GPT-6 Astra + codex at O-EVAL 64.58 2.93 and MULTI-BO 1.132, Fable 5.1 + claude-code at 63.11 1.33 and 1.081, means over three seeds), while the $2.54 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash + opencode holds 59.81 1.25 at 1/100 the cost; varying only the harness moves O-EVAL by at most 0.07 pp, so the board measures the model rather than the harness. Per-seed deviations reach 2.9 pp, so adjacent rows are not significantly separated. One case study inverts the usual story: on dragondance the models were right and our anchor was wrongthe sharpest argument for independently checkable feasibility.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent and assistant benchmarks. Softwareengineering and terminal agents are measured by repository-level tasks (SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024)) and end-to-end command-line tasks (Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026)); assistants by tool-use suites such as GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024) and τ -bench (Yao et al., 2025). Machinelearning and data-science agents are measured on Kaggle-style pipelines (Chan et al., 2025; Starace et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). These capture tool use and long-horizon execution in containerthe harness we build onbut score leaderboard position or rubric over deliverable, never modeling artifact, and attach no feasibility contract. Mathematical and optimization reasoning. Closed-form mathematics benchmarks measure deduction, not modeling (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Cobbe et al., 2021; Glazer et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2022). Operations-research systems parse word problems into solver-ready formulations and evaluate optimality or feasibility of given formulation (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2024; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Mostajabdaveh et al., 2025; Lima et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025). They supply strong execution-validity precedenta solver certifies solution is feasible or optimal for stated 2 Table 1: The closest mathematical-modeling benchmarks. Only TB-MathModel combines complete contest problem, an agentic terminal run, an executable verifier, physical-feasibility checking, and machine-checkable proof, on multimodal task (Judge: LLM grades report; Solver: solver checks one formal artifact). Benchmark #Tasks #Fig. Evaluation signal Agentic Physical Lean Multimodal Mamo (Huang et al., 2025b) ModelingBench (Qian et al., 2025) MM-Bench (Liu et al., 2025) TB-MathModel (ours) 1209 68 111 18 21 Solver check LLM judge LLM judge Executable verifier Figure 1: Why modeling is hard to evaluate, and what TB-MathModel changes. (a) In the status quo an LLM judge grades report on organisation while the numbers are never checked. (b) TB-MathModel runs the problem, attachments, and figures in terminal container, requires one structured artifact, scores it one-sidedly against an O-award reproduction, and verifies feasibility with gate and Lean certificatesso plausible-but-infeasible answer is caught. modelbut cannot certify that the model captures the right abstraction, and none requires assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or defended recommendation. benchmarks Mathematical-modeling and agents. The closest work forms continuum, and none of it is simultaneously agentic, verifiable, and terminal. Mamo (Huang et al., 2025b) is solver-grounded: models emit solver-consumable artifacts and the solver is falsifiable checker, giving precise but narrow signal on formal fragments rather than whole contest problems. ModelingAgent and its ModelingBench (Qian et al., 2025) are report-level: open-ended problems graded by an expert-style LLM judgeecologically rich but judge-calibration dependent and non-reproducible. MM-Agent and MM-Bench (Liu et al., 2025) add hierarchical modeling library, yet their primary evaluation remains report rubric. TB-MathModel keeps the full contest statement and the agentic workflow, pins evaluation to structured artifact scored by an executable verifier, and adds feasibility layer neither camp provides. Verification in evaluation. Theorem provers such as Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) with Mathlib (The mathlib Community, 2020) have certified competition and research mathematics, and RL over formal proof has produced strong provers (Hubert et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2024). Using prover not to find answers but to audit benchmarks own feasibility decisions is, to our knowledge, new: our Lean layer re-proves the programmatic gates invariants, so an assertion becomes machine-checkable fact (Sutton, 2001), at integer-and-rational arithmetic cost the kernel decides without the full library. Multimodal agents and reproduction-anchored scoring. Tool-using agents increasingly externalize their state for reuse (Yao et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026). TB3 MathModel makes visual evidence load-bearing figures are cropped from the official PDFsso harnesses with and without an image channel can be compared on identical tasks. Anchoring numerical benchmark on published solution is standard practice; we show it creates three under-reported hazards (direction asymmetry, degenerate scoring bands, unpinned units) and give auditable rules and tests for each.

sections.title: 3 The TB-MathModel Benchmark
sections.content: TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench) turns each contest problem into self-contained terminal task. Figure 2 summarises the construction pipeline. build script assembles the official contest material into four parts: (i) an instruction file with the verbatim statement and its figures; (ii) an agent container holding the mirrored attachments and an output schema; (iii) separate verifier container holding the scoring panel and an executable feasibility check; and (iv) an oracle that reproduces the Outstanding-award (O-award) paper. The agent is dropped into the terminal with this material and must return single structured artifact. Everything downstream of the artifact scoring and feasibilityis machine-executable. Task selection and sources. TB-MathModel comprises 18 tasks: the A, B, and problems of CUMCM and MCM for each of 20232025. We restrict to the last three years on purpose: older problems predate capable LLMs and were calibrated to software-assistant graders, so their task mix and review standard differ from the post-LLM regime, and recent editions are harder and more discriminating. The two contests complement each other CUMCM is engineering/optimization-heavy and Chinese, MCM is modeling-flavored and English and taking all three problems of each year covers the standard = physical/engineering, = data/optimization, = data-science split without cherry-picking. Statements and attachments are mirrored verbatim; statements figures are cropped from the official PDF (artwork plus its caption) and delivered inline and at stable container paths. 21 unique figures across 6 tasks are load-bearing: the statements reference them for geometry not restated in text (e.g., the dragon-dance U-turn curve, which fixes the final head speed), so harness without an image channel cannot recover ithence the multimodal evaluation. TBMathModel is pure evaluation set, with no training split or difficulty tiering (Appendix A). The artifact contract and oracle anchors. The scored object is one JSON file per task, whose schema (field names and types only) is shipped to the agent; extra CSV/XLSX/PNG artifacts are not scored. schema-constrained JSON is what makes an automated score possible, at the cost of mapping free-form effort onto named numeric fieldsa tension we revisit in Section 4.3. Each task is anchored to one O-award paper, re-implemented as script that reads the attachments and emits the same JSON; the reproduction is the normalisation endpoint (O-EVAL = 100%) and sets the per-metric panel, coverage 18/18. Provenance is first-class fieldpaper id, PDF/OCR source, and reproduction scopeso any anchor can be re-derived (Appendix D); this is what let us catch and correct an infeasible dragon-dance anchor before it reached the board. 3.1 Scoring: direction-aware, one-sided, auditable naive distance-to-anchor metric silently rewards copying and punishes improvement, so TB-MathModel scores each task through permetric panel with an explicit semantic direction. Each task ships panel of 26 scored metrics (60 in total), each with path into the artifact, an anchor value O, direction, and weight. metric is higher_is_better, lower_is_better, target_value (closest to wins), or exact_value, set from the modeling semantics of the quantity rather than the sign of its value. Directional metrics use an asymmetric, onesided reward: meeting or beating the anchor never scores below 1.0, so improving on the paper is never punished (full formulas in Appendix G). Three failure modes recur often enough to deserve named rules. (i) Degenerate bands: band narrower than 2% of the value magnitude cannot discriminate, so we widen it to 5%this changed one cell (stair-wear, 72.67 73.52). (ii) Noncomparable units: when an anchor is an arbitrary raw index with no schema-pinned unit (a hostfish index of 1080), model reporting the same quantity normalised to [0, 1] is not wrong, so such metrics are dropped for every model and the oracle by configuration-only rule. (iii) Cardinality mismatch: surplus items are excluded rather than counted missing. Build: official statements, attachments, and PDF figures are compiled into task directory. Run: the agent works inside network-isolated terminal container and writes one JSON artifact. Evaluate: the artifact is scored by direction-aware, one-sided panel against an O-award reproduction, and independently checked by programmatic feasibility gate plus Lean 4 certificate layer; failed gate zeroes the task. with the reason recorded. Let R, , be the weighted panel raw of submission, of the DeepSeek V4 Flash baseline, and of the oracle. We report O-EVAL = clamp(R/O, 0, 1) averaged over tasks (the headline absolute score) and gap-compensated ROBUST BO-EVAL = clip((R )/(O ), 1) when the oraclebaseline gap exceeds 0.10, and the clipped raw gain otherwise, with ROBUST BO-EVAL = 1 for missing artifact (full formulas in Appendix G). TBMathModel instead asks every human expert. For each task we extracted the final-question values reported by all available Outstanding-award papers for that problem, giving 99 panel papers, 94 of which yield the scored quantity. Coverage is 18/18 tasks and all available outstanding papers are used1 to 18 per task (median 4), since the number of O-award reports differs by problem. Each paper is one vote. Let (t) be the scored metrics of task t, (t) its paper panel, and Sp (t) the fields paper actually reports. Each paper thus contributes exactly how close is the model to this human answer, on the fields that human reported. Because R(p, Sp) = 1, every paper agrees with itself and the reproduction reproduces the panel. Equal weighting keeps one human solution to one vote, and paper that reports only single field acts as single-field check rather than being discardedthe honest treatment of an incomplete report. paper is never silently dropped. When it cannot supply the scored quantity it carries machine-readable exclusion_reason, of which number_only_in_figure, five forms occur: figure_only_logistic_prior, figure_only, no_numeric_estimate, and different_unit_of_analysis; these account for the 5 of 99 papers outside the panel. Values are never interpolated or adjusted toward the existing anchor, and papers different-but-equivalent unit is converted explicitly and noted. Where panel is emptypossible when an MCM answer is prose or figure onlythe task falls back to the single reproduced anchor, and missing artifact scores 0, so the denominator is always the fixed 18 tasks. panel also makes disagreement between humans visible instead of hiding it behind one anchor. On mcm-2024-c-tennis-momentum, 10 of 11 outstanding papers conclude that momentum is supported while the reproduced anchoritself an O-award reportconcludes it is not; on that task model scores 0.909 if it answers with the majority and 0.091 if it matches the anchor, so the score reflects which valid statistical test the model chose rather than modeling quality. We mark such literature-split tasks explicitly and exclude them from any headline ranking, while keeping them in the panel: they are the clearest evidence that single-anchor score would have been arbitrary. Relative to the single-anchor board, this changes ROBUST BO-EVAL into multi-reference gain index against the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash baseline, anchored at 1.0: MULTI-BO = 1 + clip (cid:18) Ot ft 1 ft (cid:19) , 1, +1 , (2) with ft the Flash score on task and Ot the models, averaged over tasks; when the remaining headroom 1 ft is below 0.10 we fall back to 1 + clip(Ot ft, 0.10), and missing artifact scores 1. value of 1.0 therefore means level with Flash, 1.08 means closed 8% of the remaining gap to the human panel; it is ratio, not percentage, and is not comparable to O-EVAL. 3.3 Feasibility verification: two layers Proximity to an anchor does not imply that an answer is physically admissible: submission can match reference value on one field while violating stated constraint on another. TB-MathModel verifies feasibility independently of scoring, in two layers with different trust bases. Layer 1: programmatic gate over six decidable forms. Every task registers one feasibility check, and the registry covers 18/18 tasks; every 6 hard-error branch falls into one of six decidable forms (Appendix Table 12). Checks are either structural/domain bounds (rates, correlations, probabilities, non-negative counts, distributions summing to 100, peak average) or constraint replay (heliostat rated power 60 MW and installation height [2, 6] m, dragon-dance head speed amplification ratio 2 m/s, demand-capped revenue ceiling, union duration the sum of its parts). Three contracts keep the gate honest: coverage (a task cannot ship ungated), oracle self-consistency (the O-award reference must pass its own check), and discrimination (synthetic and real-field violations must be rejected, while an empty artifact warns rather than hard-fails). Four constraints that need an independent replay rather than field check are recorded as whole-task penalties (Appendix G). Layer 2: Lean certificates. To make the gates own correctness checkable, Layer 2 re-proves the same invariants as Lean 4 theorems, so the audit rests on the kernel. It generates 624 obligations across all 18 tasks, discharged by decide or omega. No Mathlib is usedthe propositions are decidable on exact integersand values are scaled to integers, so there is no floating-point tolerance; the one exception, composite index, is declared in the predicate because the tolerance is itself part of the audited assumption. trust audit (#print axioms) reports only [propext, Quot.sound] or none, with no sorryAx and no native_decide (grep-checked). discrimination suite mutates one numeric leaf at time and requires the build to fail and to cite the field; ten mutations across all six forms are rejected. Two soft warnings become proofs: tourism acceptance index is refuted for the unit convention, and sustainability score fits neither convention within declared budget. Verification scope. The two layers decide every feasibility question that structured artifact can settle without model of the physics (Appendix Table 13): unit/value ranges (A) and internal consistency (B). Whether the reported value reflects real physical truth (C)does the field really produce 60 MW?is property of the world rather than of the artifact, so TB-MathModel verifies it where the problem admits an independent replay. Within this scope the layers are exact: any obligation whose evidence is absent is reported as witnessed gap rather than silently satisfied, so the audit never overstates what it has proved.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Setup We evaluate seven multimodal model/harness entries, whose harness can open the cropped figures. Each entry is run with three seeds per task and reported as mean with standard deviation; where model was run at two reasoning tiers we keep the higher-scoring variant. Every row is scored with the same scorer and current anchors, so the board shares one scoring definition (Appendix C). The prompt is the tasks instruction file, passed verbatim: the contest statement, the cited figures inline, and fixed Required Benchmark Artifact block naming the output path (Appendix E). Tasks run in Docker containerspython:3.12-slim with fixed scientific stack, internet disabled, model traffic through local retry proxyso an agent cannot fetch solutions or install packages at run time; limits are 2 CPUs, 8 GB, no GPU, and 4-hour timeout (Appendix B). Each multimodal entry is run three times per task and reported as mean with standard deviation; the one wellposed task, dragon-dance, is additionally probed four times, where the answers agreed to machine precision (std=4.6 1016). 4.2 Main result: the multimodal board Table 2 is the main result: the seven multimodal entries on all 18 tasks, each three-seed mean ( std); the per-entry configuration is in Appendix Table 7. O-EVAL is the primary metric: the multireference score of Section 3.2, i.e. the mean over the human paper panel of how close the model is to each accepted answer. MULTI-BO is the secondary, relative index of that same score against the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash baseline, fixed at 1.000 cell-by-cell: 1.08 means the model closed 8% of Flashs remaining gap to the panel, so it is read against the baseline and is not percentage. Five findings stand out. 1. The newest flagships lead. GPT-6 Astra + codex (64.58 2.93) and Fable 5.1 + claudecode (63.11 1.33) top the board, about 4.8 and 3.4 points above GPT-5.5 xhigh + codex (59.75 1.55), and both clear the Flash baseline by 13.2% and 8.1% of the remaining gap respectively. 2. Cost buys real but bounded gap. The two leaders cost $246$273 per run, while the cheapest strong entry, DeepSeek-Flash + opencode, reaches 59.81 1.25 at $2.54about 4.8 points behind the leader at roughly 1/100 the cost. 3. Cheap open models cluster below the flagships. Among the low-cost entries DeepSeekFlash (59.81), Kimi K3 (58.23), GLM-5.3 (57.78), and Qwen3.8 Flash (52.66) span about 7 points, and only the two flagships exceed the baseline index (1.132 and 1.081); DeepSeekFlash defines it at 1.000 and every other entry falls below. 4. small gap is not yet resolved ranking. Perseed deviations reach 2.93 pp, so the 1.5 pp separation between the two leaders and between GPT-5.5 and Flash sits inside one standard deviation; we report the order but do not claim significant difference between adjacent rows. 5. More inference compute is not monotone. Running DeepSeek-Flash at its maximum reasoning tier drops its multi-reference score to 48.11% and its MULTI-BO to 0.864, well below the default tiers 59.81 and 1.000, at higher cost: larger deliberative budget does not simply buy accuracy on these tasks. Hard gate and cost. The gate removes exactly the cells whose answers violate stated constraint and leaves the ranking otherwise stable, so it is surgical rather than blanket penalty. Cost is dominated by per-token price, not usage: GPT-5.5s $99.37 is mostly cache-read input and output at roughly 33/50 DeepSeek V4.1 Flashs rates, despite comparable token counts. Three patterns stand out. (a) The CUMCMMCM gap is large and modeldependent. For the weaker entries, CUMCM cells sit near 100% while MCM cells sit between 0% and 60%: the engineering problems have welldefined final numbers most models reach, whereas MCM problems are more open and their anchors more contestable. The strongest entries narrow the gap only slightly (GPT-6 82.9 on CUMCM vs. 46.2 on MCM; GPT-5.5 79.7 vs. 39.8). sizeable share of tasks is now solved near-perfectly expected of current benchmarkand the boards discrimination comes from the open-ended MCM (b) Two tasks are all-or-nothing. problems. On mcm-2024-b-submersible every entry scores 100%, while on mcm-2024-c-tennis even the flagships score below 40%. Such tasks either fall inside or outside the panels tolerance entirely, so they separate regimes of models but not models within one. (c) Many low scores reflect reference scale/scope, not modeling error. Several tasks contain metric whose model/panel ratio exceeds 5: host-fish index reported near 1080 by some papers while models give normalised [0, 1] quantity; sustainability score near 1.007 against models reporting 0100 utility; 6 6 grid against models discretising the same region into hundreds of cells; and 72.67 73.52 band in which the papers own baseline scores zero. Scoring pitfalls we found and fixed. An anchorbased benchmark is only as credible as its anchors, so we audited every scoring rule and anchor and report what the audit changed (Appendix G). Two gate false positives were removed without moving any score, and degenerate-band widening affected one cell (+0.35 pp). Excluding two noncomparable-unit metrics raised every entry by 0.05 8 2.62 ppthe signature of systematic scoring effect rather than model difference. Most consequentially, the audit flagged the dragon-dance anchor as physically infeasible and we corrected it (Section 4.2). What the feasibility layers caught. The gate hard-invalidated 7 cells, concentrated on heliostat (rated power below 60 MW, or mirror below the 2 minimum) plus single cells for smoke-screen, Juneau, and Olympic. The Lean layer turns two soft warnings into proofs and proves non-vacuity by accepting corrected artifact under the predicate that rejects the reported one. On the one numerically well-posed task the runs agree to machine precision, and across the board the per-seed deviations stay small relative to the spread between entries  (Table 2)  , so rankings do not depend on the seed. 4.4 From Findings to Model Development TB-MathModel is meant to improve models, not only rank them. Three levers follow from the findings above, and each is trainable with signals TBMathModel already produces. Verified reward for RL. The feasible, oraclenormalised score is an executable, reproducible rewardevery submission passes the gate and the Lean layer. Rejection-sampling (keep and rank gate-accepted trajectories by O-EVAL) works today; group-relative policy optimisation with the gate as hard multiplier teaches the model to satisfy the physics before chasing the reference. The dragon-dance case motivates this: twelve models computed the right peak but were penalised, so what they lack is self-checkingexactly what verifier in the reward provides. Targets against the observed failures. Finding (a)the open-ended MCM suite separates quality while CUMCM saturatessays to train assumptions, formulation, and sensitivity rather than closed-form solving; finding (c)many losses are unit and scale mismatchessays to state and verify units, ranges, and schema before emitting number. Both are rewarded directly by the artifact contract. Feasibility the artifact can check. The dragondance audit exposes the failure value-range check cannot: consistent answer that is physically inadmissible because the artifact omits the evidence (no per-mirror layout, no peak-neighbourhood sample). Training models to emit that witness raises the score and makes them checkable, reaching level C. 9 Case studies. Three rolesa top proprietary agent, the oracle, and the low-cost open agentare compared on three problems in Appendix F. On dragon-dance all three converge while the papers value is the infeasible outlier, so the models were right and our anchor was wrong. On crop-planting the papers constraints are jointly infeasible, so we anchor on reproducible exact MILP optimum. On Juneau the sustainability score is reported on different unit scales, which is why the task schema, not the scorer, must pin fields range.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented TB-MathModel, the first agentic and verifiable terminal benchmark of 18 real mathematical-modeling problems, distinguished by direction-aware, one-sided scoring that never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification combining gate over six decidable invariant forms with 624 kernel-checked Lean obligations. Scoring each task against panel of human outstanding papers, the newest flagships lead across seven multimodal entries (GPT-6 Astra at O-EVAL 64.58%, Fable 5.1 at 63.11%), while the $2.54 open DeepSeek-Flash holds 59.81% at 1/100 the cost. We documented the scoring pitfalls we fixed, and showed case where the benchmark itself was wrong and the models were right. The two-layer design is the transferable idea: fast gate covers every task and proof assistant makes the audits own correctness machinecheckable, while stating what neither can answer. Because TB-MathModel gives reproducible reward, its trajectories are also training material, and Section 4.4 turns the findings into directions.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: TB-MathModel normalises each task against reproducible Outstanding-award solution, with peranchor provenance so any reference can be rederived; because modeling admits no single correct answer, the natural extension is multi-paper panel reporting spread over accepted solutions. The two verification layers decide every feasibility question structured artifact can settle (unit/value ranges and internal consistency); external physical truth is property of the world, so it is checked where problem admits an independent replay, and any obligation whose evidence is missing is reported rather than silently passed. Panel size varies with the number of outstanding reports per problem (1 to 18 papers), and where humans themselves disagreeas on the tennis momentum test, where 10 of 11 papers reach the opposite conclusion from the anchorwe mark the task literature-split and keep it out of headline rankings. Scores are threeseed means, and the task shell carries over to engineering and cross-disciplinary problems.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Statements, attachments, and figures are official CUMCM and MCM material used for research evaluation; we do not redistribute Outstandingaward solutions, and reproduction code derives from public corpus with per-task provenance. Users should confirm the licence terms for their own redistribution. TB-MathModel measures and improves the modeling workflow of LLM agents rather than automating work presented as teams own, and entirely automated evaluation keeps the cost of broad participation low.

sections.title: Use of Large Language Models
sections.content: LLMs served as the systems under testevery entry in Table 2 is an LLM agent, which is the object of measurementand as writing assistants that helped draft prose and check the internal consistency of LATEX and numbers. Benchmark construction, scoring rules, feasibility checks, and Lean obligations were specified, implemented, and verified by the authors, and all numerical results are produced by the released scripts.

sections.content: C.1 Per-entry configuration and results Table 7 lists the seven multimodal entries with the harness and reasoning tier actually passed and their full scores. Multimodal status means the harness exposes an image channel. Every entry is run with three seeds per task. C.2 Agent command templates The task statement is passed to the agent as its prompt. Representative commands from the recorded trials: # codex codex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --skipgit-repo-check --model gpt-5.5 --json --enable unified_exec -c model_reasoning_effort=xhigh -- '<instruction.md body>' # opencode opencode --model=openai/deepseek-flash run --format=json -- thinking --dangerously-skip-permissions -- '<instruction.md body>' Each CLI harness receives the statement as its positional prompt; the harness prepends its own generic system prompt before it. C.3 Retries, concurrency, and artifact recovery All entries used one concurrent trial and no automatic retries; each of the three seeds is an independent pass over the 18 tasks. Two subtleties are disclosed. First, misfiled artifacts: two tasks wrote the result with hyphen instead of the required underscore, so the harness did not collect it; we replayed the recorded runs scripts to reproduce the artifact and re-scored it. Second, third-party runs: the GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 entries were run by independent operators; because their verifier used different reward formula, we re-scored their saved artifacts with our scorer and current anchors so that all entries share one scoring definition. Where an artifact was not packaged, we reconstructed the scored fields from the saved permetric records, verified to reproduce the operators own numbers exactly on the tasks where the full artifact was present. C.4 Cost accounting Cost is computed from measured token usage against fixed price snapshot, with two conservative adjustments stated in the report: reasoning tokens that provider bills outside its completion counter are added to output, and where provider charges peak/off-peak rate, the peak rate is used. For the two third-party entries, cost is their own measured per-run USD. Because the pricing file is local and fixed, costs do not drift between reruns.

sections.title: E Prompt Design
sections.content: E.4 Version caveat E.1 The prompt is the task statement There is no hand-written prompt wrapper in this benchmark. The prompt is the tasks instruction file, delivered verbatim by the harness. Its structure is fixed across tasks: machine-readable canary comment (stripped before delivery); an Original Contest Problem section containing the verbatim statement with each cited figure embedded inline; any results tables the statement requires, as plain text; note listing the in-container figure paths; Required Benchmark Artifact section; and the time-limit line. E.2 The artifact block (verbatim template) # Required Benchmark Artifact Solve the contest problem above. The official attachments are mirrored at `/root/data/attachments` (flat filenames; see `/root/data/attachments/INDEX.md`) and also remain at their full corpus paths under `/root/data/repo`. Use them whenever they are relevant. Write your final structured answer to: /root/results/<slug>_result.json The result must be valid JSON and should follow the shape shown in `/root/data/output_schema.json`. Include the numerical quantities, modeling decisions, diagnostics, sensitivity or uncertainty results, conclusions for the contest questions, and generated artifact paths needed to support your answer. You may also write supplementary CSV, XLSX, or PNG files under `/root/results`, but the JSON file above is the required artifact. You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task. E.3 Harness wrapping The harnesses deliver the same text differently. Each CLI harness prepends its own generic command-line system prompt and then supplies the statement as the positional prompt. The instruction files were revised after some trials were recorded: figure-path section was added, and one MCM statement was re-sourced from the official PDF. The prompt actually delivered in given trial is the one captured in that trials log; for reproducibility, cite those, not the current file. This is why we describe the prompt structure above rather than quoting todays file as if it were what every model saw. E.5 What the prompt withholds by design By design the prompt is pure task description: no modeling hints, no method suggestions, and no pointer to the scored fields beyond the schema. It leaves the agent to infer which numbers matter, which keeps the setting test of the whole modeling problem rather than fill-in-the-schema exercise. This keeps the benchmark test of doing the whole modeling problem, at the cost of the agent having to infer which numbers matter. Case Studies (Full Numerics) We give the full per-field comparison for the three case studies. Values are read from each roles saved artifact; the oracle column is the anchor. All three tables span both columns. The reconstruction of the true peak is continuous-time maximum of the handle-speed ratio; the paper sampled integer seconds and stepped over it. The exact identity head_speedratio= 2 m/s, checked by both the programmatic gate and the Lean layer, is what exposes the paper value as infeasible: the papers isolated value 1.406276 m/s (with ratio 1.422195) implies 2.2568 m/s at handle. The papers full constraint set is infeasible on the official attachments, so the anchor is reproducible MILP optimum and the models plans sit in the same regime. The anchor lies between the two 17 Table 9: Dragon-dance (CUMCM 2024 A, Q5). All three roles agree; the paper value is the outlier and is infeasible. Quantity Oracle (anchor) GPT-5.5 DeepSeek V4.1 max_head_speed_mps max_speed_ratio 1.246266 1.604793 1.24626636 1.60479338 1.24626636 1.60479338 Table 10: Crop-planting (CUMCM 2024 C, Q1). Special case: the anchor is reproducible exact optimum under the papers per-plot cap. Quantity (yuan, 7-year) Anchor (exact MILP) GPT-5.5 DeepSeek V4. waste-surplus profit 50%-discount profit 40,418,877 58,718,967 40,320,587 66,485,662 41,559,515 70,378,276 models on the discount column, which is why single scalar cannot summarise this task. This is the clearest scale problem. The anchor is on 1 unit scale; one third-party agent reports the same field on 0100 multiattribute utility scale that it explicitly declares in its own artifact. Because the tasks output schema does not pin the range, the agent is not wrongwhich is why the correct repair is to specify the fields range in the schema, not to rescale in the scorer. F.1 Discussion Dragon-dance. The papers isolated value (1.406276) is the wrong one. This case matters most because it inverts the usual story: the models were right and the reference was wrong, and the fix was to the benchmark. It also shows why the feasibility layer is not redundant with scoringratio head speed = 2 m/s is an exact identity that both layers check, and it is what made the paper values infeasibility visible. Crop-planting. GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek produce plan profits in the same regime, and the optimum sits between them on one columnwhich is why single scalar cannot summarise the task. When the human paper is not reproducible, the honest move is to anchor on reproducible value and mark it, not to penalise models for matching an irreproducible number. Juneau. The oracle recommends an 11,000/day cap at 55 USD with sustainability score of 1.007, GPT-5.5 recommends 20,000/day at 20 USD on its own 01 scale, and DeepSeek recommends 16,000/day at 30 USD. This argues that the task schemanot just the scorermust state fields range and units, which is fix to the task rather than to the code.

Across the 18 tasks there are 60 scored metrics; one further Wordle metric is declared at weight 0 and recorded but excluded from the panel. The per-task counts are in Table 5. G.3 Excluded metrics Two metrics are excluded from the panel for every model and the oracle, both by configuration-only rules: the Olympic fourth recommendation (the prompt asks for three countries but the reproduction emits four rows), and the two lamprey raw population indices when the anchor magnitude exceeds 5 (the anchor is an arbitrary raw index with no schema-pinned unit). G.4 Hard-gate decisions Seven whole-task penalties were applied across the entries: four heliostat violations (rated power below 60 MW, or mirror below the 2 minimum), one smoke-screen plan failing an independent coverage replay, one Juneau answer with unit-invalid acceptance/sustainability values, and one Olympic answer with degenerate coach-effect result. G.5 Pitfalls found and fixed An anchor-based benchmark is only as credible as its anchors, so we audited the scoring rules and anchors and report what the audit changed. Two gate false positives (a signed elasticity read as negative count; missing field read as hard contradiction) were corrected but changed no score, and degenerate-band widening moved one score (+0.35 pp for v4 pro). Non-comparable-unit exclusion raised every entry by 0.052.62 pp, since the penalty applied to all submissions equally the signature of systematic scoring error rather than model difference. Finally, the dragondance anchor was itself physically infeasible: the papers 1.406276 m/s would drive handle to 1.406276 1.604793 = 2.2568 m/s, above the 2 m/s cap, because it maximised over integer seconds and stepped over the true continuous-time peak at = 14.48 s. We corrected the anchor to 1.246266 m/s; twelve of the evaluated models had reported the correct value and had been sitting at 49.82%, while the two matching the erroneous paper value had been at 100%. Here the benchmark, not the model, was wrong (Appendices and H). G.6 Degenerate-band and validity rules The band-widening rule applies to the endpoint metrics of the three endpoint-style tasks. Applying all scoring fixes in this paper moved every entry upward by 0.052.62 pp, because the affected penalties applied to all submissions equallythe diagnostic signature of systematic scoring error rather than model difference.
